title: The Merchant of Venice
author: William Shakespeare
setting: Venice — the Rialto, a private house, a court of justice — and Belmont, a country estate a day's journey away
lengthNote: Around 2,600 lines, of which the trial takes nearly four hundred
openingLine: In sooth, I know not why I am so sad:
summary: A merchant borrows money he does not need, on terms he thinks are a joke, so that a friend can go courting. The comedy that follows has a courtroom at its centre, and the clever rescue there is also a confiscation: Shylock loses his money, his profession and his religion in the space of forty lines, and the play then moves to a moonlit garden and refuses to mention him again.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of The Merchant of Venice
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering, which counts the prose scenes continuously. Modern editions vary.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Topical references and the style of the verse place composition in the later 1590s.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: The First Quarto, which remains the basis of most modern editions.

atAGlance.label: Chief source
atAGlance.note: The bond, the trial and the disguised lady-lawyer come from a tale in Ser Giovanni Fiorentino's Italian collection.

atAGlance.label: At court
atAGlance.note: The first recorded performance was on 10 February 1605, and the play was repeated before the court two days later.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: Antonio’s sadness, Portia’s caskets and the bond
structure.summary: Antonio cannot say why he is unhappy. Bassanio needs money to court an heiress whose father has left her unable to choose her own husband, and Shylock lends it on a forfeit of a pound of flesh — proposed, and accepted, as a piece of friendly humour by men who have just insulted each other.

scenes.title: The Rialto
scenes.summary: Antonio's friends try to explain his melancholy; Bassanio asks for a further loan to go to Belmont.

scenes.title: The will of a dead father
scenes.summary: Portia reviews her suitors with Nerissa and complains of a lottery she cannot refuse.

scenes.title: The merry bond
scenes.summary: Shylock recalls years of public abuse, then lends interest-free against a pound of Antonio's flesh.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: Morocco and Arragon, and Jessica’s flight
structure.summary: Morocco and Arragon choose gold and silver and are beaten by their own assumptions about worth. In Venice, Jessica leaves her father’s house dressed as a boy, taking money and jewels with her, and the Christian gentlemen of the Rialto treat Shylock’s public grief as street entertainment.

scenes.title: Morocco arrives
scenes.summary: He asks not to be judged by his complexion and is told the terms of the lottery.

scenes.title: Launcelot changes master
scenes.summary: The clown argues with his own conscience and leaves Shylock for Bassanio.

scenes.title: Jessica's plan
scenes.summary: She calls her father's house hell and asks Launcelot to carry a letter to Lorenzo.

scenes.title: The masque
scenes.summary: Lorenzo learns what gold and jewels she will bring with her.

scenes.title: Locking up
scenes.summary: Shylock, going out to supper against his judgement, tells Jessica to shut the windows.

scenes.title: The elopement
scenes.summary: Jessica throws down a casket and escapes in boy's clothes, ashamed of the disguise.

scenes.title: Gold
scenes.summary: Morocco opens the golden casket and finds a skull and a rhyme about glittering.

scenes.title: Reported grief
scenes.summary: Salanio performs Shylock's cries about his daughter and his ducats for laughs.

scenes.title: Silver
scenes.summary: Arragon takes what he deserves and is handed the portrait of a blinking idiot.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Bassanio chooses lead, and Antonio’s ships are lost
structure.summary: Bassanio rejects ornament, chooses lead and wins Portia within the hour. In the same act Shylock, taunted in the street about his daughter, answers with the play's most famous demand for common humanity and ends it by promising revenge. News arrives that Antonio's ships are gone.

scenes.title: On the Rialto
scenes.summary: Salarino and Salanio bait Shylock; Tubal brings news of Jessica's spending and of a wrecked argosy.

scenes.title: Lead
scenes.summary: Bassanio chooses correctly; the rings are given; a letter from Antonio interrupts the betrothal.

scenes.title: No more speaking
scenes.summary: Shylock refuses to hear Antonio and repeats that he will have his bond.

scenes.title: Padua
scenes.summary: Portia sends for legal papers from Doctor Bellario and tells Nerissa they will go disguised.

scenes.title: Salvation and bacon
scenes.summary: Launcelot jokes that converting Jews will raise the price of pork; Jessica changes the subject.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: The trial
structure.summary: The longest scene in the play. Shylock refuses three times the money, Portia arrives disguised as a lawyer from Padua and preaches mercy, and then wins by reading the bond more strictly than its holder. Within forty lines Shylock has lost his estate, his livelihood and his religion.

scenes.title: The trial
scenes.summary: Mercy is argued, the bond is enforced to the letter, and an alien statute is produced against the plaintiff.

scenes.title: The rings
scenes.summary: Portia and Nerissa, still disguised, collect the rings their husbands swore never to part with.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Belmont, and the rings
structure.summary: Lorenzo and Jessica trade stories of lovers who came to bad ends, the wives expose the business of the rings, and Antonio learns that three of his ships are safe after all. Shylock is not mentioned. The comedy closes with everybody paired except the merchant it is named after.

scenes.title: Moonlight
scenes.summary: Music, the ring quarrel, the revelation of the disguise, and news that Antonio's argosies have come home.

characters.name: Shylock
characters.summary: He appears in five scenes and dominates the play. Shakespeare gives him the abuse he has taken in detail — the spitting, the name-calling, the kicks — and then has him use that history as a legal instrument. The play neither excuses what he does nor lets his enemies off the account he reads them.
characters.clue: He keeps a ledger of insults as exactly as one of debts, asks whether a dog has money, and leaves the stage saying he is not well.

characters.name: Portia
characters.summary: Rich, quick and confined: her father's will means she may neither choose nor refuse. She takes the only freedom available by leaving Belmont in a man's gown, and the same intelligence that saves Antonio is later used to trap her own husband over a ring.
characters.clue: She may neither choose a husband nor refuse one, so she borrows a lawyer's gown from Padua and wins the biggest case in Venice.
traits: less merciful than her own speech

relationships.label: rescuer of, and rival for Bassanio
prosecutes in the guise of defending

characters.name: Antonio
characters.summary: The title character speaks the first line of the play and almost nothing in the last scene. His sadness is never explained; his willingness to die for Bassanio is stated plainly, and so is his intention to go on spitting on Shylock. He is the only major figure who ends the play unpaired.
characters.clue: He opens the play saying he does not know why he is sad, offers his own body as security for a friend's courtship, and ends it the only one without a partner.

characters.name: Bassanio
characters.summary: He has run through his money and proposes to repair it by marrying a fortune, which he explains to Antonio without embarrassment. His casket speech rejects outward show in terms that apply uncomfortably well to his own courtship, financed by a borrowed appearance of wealth.
characters.clue: He argues that the world is deceived by ornament while wearing clothes bought with a friend's borrowed money.

characters.name: Jessica
characters.summary: She robs her father, sells her mother's ring for a monkey, and converts. Shakespeare gives her the discomfort as well as the escape: she is ashamed of her boy's clothes, and in the last act she and Lorenzo exchange a string of stories about lovers whose nights ended badly.
characters.clue: She leaves her father's house in a boy's coat with his ducats in a casket, and spends the last act naming lovers who came to grief.

characters.name: Lorenzo
characters.role: A friend of Bassanio and Antonio
characters.summary: He plans the elopement as a raid, is pleased about the gold, and then speaks the play's most beautiful verse about music and the harmony of the spheres. The distance between those two facts is one of the things the last act is for.
characters.clue: He organises a theft and an elopement in the same breath, and later explains that a man with no music in him is fit for treasons.

characters.name: Nerissa
characters.summary: She doubles Portia at every level: she gives the sceptical answer in 1.2, marries the friend, not the principal, disguises herself as a clerk, and runs the same trick with the same ring. The play works by these pairings, and she is the clearest of them.
characters.clue: She dresses as a lawyer’s clerk, marries the hero’s friend, and plays the ring trick a second time.

characters.name: Gratiano
characters.summary: Bassanio says he speaks an infinite deal of nothing, and for three acts that is a joke about a harmless talker. In the courtroom he becomes the voice that cheers each reversal and asks for Shylock to be hanged, which is where the comic licence stops being comic.
characters.clue: A friend says he speaks an infinite deal of nothing; in court he applauds every turn of the verdict and offers the defeated man a free halter.

themes.name: Bonds and binding
themes.summary: The word runs through every plot in the play: a bond is a loan agreement, a tie of friendship, a marriage, a ring, and finally a piece of writing that can take a man's life. Venice runs on written obligation, and the tragedy is that Shylock is the only character who treats the writing as meaning exactly what it says.
themes.development: A bond is sealed in 1.3, tested in 4.1 and replaced in 5.1 by a ring — which is another bond, and also broken.

themes.name: Mercy and justice
themes.summary: Portia's argument is that mercy cannot be compelled, which is true, and she then compels Shylock into receiving it. The court offers him his life on condition that he give up his religion, and calls that leniency. The play stages the gap between the doctrine and the settlement enacted in its name.
themes.development: Mercy is preached at 4.1.191, refused by Shylock at 4.1.213, and delivered at 4.1.396 as a set of conditions including forced conversion.

themes.name: Antisemitism and the outsider
themes.summary: The Christians of Venice call Shylock dog, devil and cur to his face and in his absence, and Antonio says plainly that he will do it again. The play lets Shylock answer, at length and in prose, and then ends with his enemies in a garden and his name unmentioned.
themes.development: The abuse is itemised by its victim in 1.3, answered in 3.1, and given legal form in 4.1, where an alien is found to have no standing against a citizen.

themes.name: Worth, ornament and risk
themes.summary: Three caskets ask what a thing is worth; three suitors answer with what they think they deserve. The same question runs through the merchant plot, where ships are venture capital and a pound of flesh is valued, out loud, against mutton and beef.
themes.development: Morocco buys the outside, Arragon buys his own merit, Bassanio buys the risk — and the man who has hazarded everything has borrowed the stake.

themes.name: Friendship, marriage and rivalry
themes.summary: Antonio's feeling for Bassanio is the strongest attachment in the play and has no name available to it. Portia understands the competition exactly, which is why the ring she gives her husband is the one thing she makes him swear never to surrender, and why she has it taken from him in a courtroom.
themes.development: Antonio offers his body for Bassanio in Act I, is outbid in Act IV when Bassanio says he would give up his wife to save him, and is given a ring to return in Act V.

themes.name: Disguise and the law
themes.summary: Nothing in the trial scene is what it appears: the lawyer is a woman, the clerk is her maid, the mercy is a threat and the rescue is a confiscation. Belmont's women enter the Venetian court by the only door available to them and leave it having beaten the men at their own document.
themes.development: Jessica's boy's clothes in Act II rehearse the device; Portia's gown in Act IV makes it the machinery of the plot.

techniques.name: The legal quibble
techniques.definition: A judgment that depends on the exact words of a document, whatever its evident intention.
techniques.inThisBook: Portia defeats the bond by noting that it grants flesh and says nothing of blood — a stricter reading than Shylock's own, delivered by someone who has just argued that strictness damns us all.

techniques.name: Parallel plotting
techniques.definition: Two or more actions with the same shape, so that each comments on the other.
techniques.inThisBook: The caskets, the bond and the rings are all tests in which a man must choose what to give up, and all three are set by someone with more control than he realises.

techniques.name: Prose against verse
techniques.definition: The shift between unmetered speech and blank verse as a marker of register, class or feeling.
techniques.inThisBook: Shylock’s great answer to Salarino is in prose, which gives it the sound of a man speaking, not performing; Portia’s mercy speech is verse, and sounds like a set piece because it is one.

techniques.name: Rhetorical questions
techniques.definition: A run of questions whose answers are obvious, used to make denial impossible.
techniques.inThisBook: Eyes, hands, organs, dimensions, senses, affections, passions: the questions pile up until the last one changes direction and asks about revenge instead of about bleeding.

techniques.name: Body imagery
techniques.definition: A physical image repeated until it binds unrelated scenes together.
techniques.inThisBook: The bond's pound of flesh is only the plainest instance; Shylock calls Jessica his own flesh and blood, and the court eventually divides his property along the same line between body and estate.

techniques.name: Scriptural argument
techniques.definition: Quoting or contesting scripture as a way of settling a dispute.
techniques.inThisBook: Shylock and Antonio argue over Jacob's sheep in 1.3, each claiming the Old Testament, and Portia's mercy speech borrows the language of the Lord's Prayer to address a man who does not say it.

quotations.text: In sooth, I know not why I am so sad:
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: The opening line of the play, to Salarino and Salanio on the Rialto.
quotations.analysis: A comedy begins with a man announcing an unexplained depression, and the play never supplies the explanation — his friends propose his ships and then love, and he denies both. The refusal to account for it leaves a hole at the centre of the title role that every production has to fill with something.

quotations.text: so is the will of a living daughter curbed by the will of a dead father
quotations.speaker: Portia
quotations.context: In prose to Nerissa, listing the suitors she cannot refuse.
quotations.analysis: The sentence turns on one word used twice: 'will' as desire and 'will' as legal document. Portia’s problem is stated as a pun, which is a warning about the kind of play this is: the trial in Act IV will also be won by a word with two meanings.

quotations.text: Still have I borne it with a patient shrug, For sufferance is the badge of all our tribe.
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Answering Antonio's request for a loan by recalling how Antonio has treated him.
quotations.analysis: A badge in Venice was not a metaphor: Jews were required to wear identifying marks, and Shylock takes that fact and makes endurance itself the uniform. The shrug is the detail that does the work — a small physical gesture, repeated over years, standing in for everything he has swallowed.

quotations.text: 'Hath a dog money? is it possible A cur can lend three thousand ducats?'
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Quoting back to Antonio the names Antonio has called him.
quotations.analysis: He does not complain of the insult; he performs it, putting Antonio’s own vocabulary into a speech Antonio has to stand and listen to. Quotation marks are a weapon here: the abuse is returned intact, with the arithmetic of the loan sitting inside it.

quotations.text: I am as like to call thee so again, To spit on thee again, to spurn thee too.
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: His reply, immediately before asking for the loan anyway.
quotations.analysis: He does not deny a word of the account; he promises to repeat it. The couplet is the reason the bond is not simply a piece of villainy — the borrower has just told the lender to his face that nothing will change, and then asks to be lent the money as to an enemy.

quotations.text: Give him direction for this merry bond,
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Sending Antonio to the notary to seal the agreement.
quotations.analysis: 'Merry' is doing a great deal of work, and nobody in the scene challenges it. The forfeit is framed as a joke between men who have just exchanged threats, which is exactly what allows Antonio to sign it: a penalty that cannot be meant does not need to be feared.

quotations.text: Hie thee, gentle Jew. The Hebrew will turn Christian: he grows kind.
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: As Shylock leaves to fetch the ducats.
quotations.analysis: 'Gentle' and 'gentile' were near-homophones, so the compliment is also a joke about conversion — and the joke turns out to be a prophecy the court will enforce at knife-point in Act IV. Antonio can praise the man only by imagining him becoming someone else.

quotations.text: Our house is hell, and thou, a merry devil, Didst rob it of some taste of tediousness.
quotations.speaker: Jessica
quotations.context: Saying goodbye to Launcelot, who is leaving her father's service.
quotations.analysis: Her complaint is dullness, more than cruelty: the house is hell because it is tedious, and the clown made it bearable. It is the only account the play gives of what living with Shylock was like, and it comes from someone about to rob him.

quotations.text: All that glitters is not gold; Often have you heard that told: Many a man his life hath sold But my outside to behold:
quotations.speaker: Morocco
quotations.context: Reading the scroll found inside the golden casket, beside a skull.
quotations.analysis: The verse is in short rhyming lines, a nursery metre for a lesson everybody claims to know already, and the casket answers in the first person as though the gold were speaking. Morocco has just argued himself into gold by reasoning about what the world values — the scroll's point is that he was reasoning at all.

quotations.text: 'My daughter! O my ducats! O my daughter! Fled with a Christian! O my Christian ducats!
quotations.speaker: Salanio
quotations.context: Salanio and Salarino imitating Shylock's behaviour in the street after Jessica's flight.
quotations.analysis: The audience never sees Shylock discover the loss; it is reported as an impersonation by a man doing the voice for a laugh. Whether the alternation of daughter and ducats is grief or greed depends entirely on how far you trust the reporter, and the play deliberately gives you no other witness.

quotations.text: I am a Jew. Hath not a Jew eyes? hath not a Jew hands, organs, dimensions, senses, affections, passions? fed with the same food, hurt with the same weapons, subject to the same diseases, healed by the same means, warmed and cooled by the same winter and summer, as a Christian is?
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: In the street, to Salarino, who has just asked what a pound of flesh is good for.
quotations.analysis: The argument is built entirely on the body, not on doctrine, and the repetitions of 'the same' make the shared ground impossible to refuse. It is in prose, so it sounds like a man talking, not a set speech, and its logic is deliberately unfinished: everything so far has been about suffering, and the next sentence will apply the same equality to revenge.

quotations.text: The villany you teach me, I will execute, and it shall go hard but I will better the instruction.
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: The end of the same speech, after the questions about bleeding and laughing.
quotations.analysis: He claims to be a pupil, which puts the responsibility on the teachers and leaves him doing the thing anyway. ‘Better the instruction’ is the sentence’s cold centre: he intends to improve on Christian revenge, not merely match it, and the play holds him to that promise in the courtroom.

quotations.text: So may the outward shows be least themselves: The world is still deceived with ornament.
quotations.speaker: Bassanio
quotations.context: Deliberating in front of the three caskets at Belmont.
quotations.analysis: He wins by distrusting appearances, having arrived in Belmont on borrowed money precisely in order to look the part. 'Still' means always, and the line indicts a world Bassanio has been working rather successfully; the play lets him say the true thing without noticing that it applies to him.

quotations.text: Which is the merchant here, and which the Jew?
quotations.speaker: Portia
quotations.context: Her first words on entering the court in the gown of a doctor of laws.
quotations.analysis: The question establishes her impartiality and is also unanswerable by sight, which is the play's point about what Venice thinks it can see. She already knows which is which, so the line is a performance of neutrality by the one person in the room who has come to win.

quotations.text: The quality of mercy is not strain'd, It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven Upon the place beneath: it is twice blest; It blesseth him that gives and him that takes:
quotations.speaker: Portia
quotations.context: Answering Shylock's question: on what compulsion must he be merciful?
quotations.analysis: The whole speech depends on mercy being uncompelled, which is a direct answer to the word 'compulsion' in Shylock's question. What follows in the scene contradicts it: the court will compel mercy out of Shylock at the price of his religion, and the word for what he receives will still be mercy.

quotations.text: My deeds upon my head! I crave the law,
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Refusing Portia's appeal and asking for judgment on the bond.
quotations.analysis: He takes the consequences onto himself in the words of a formula that Shakespeare's audience would have heard as an echo of the Gospel account of Christ's condemnation, and which was used for centuries to justify persecution. Giving Shylock that sentence is the harshest thing the play does to him, and he says it in the act of asking only for what he is owed.

quotations.text: Tarry a little; there is something else. This bond doth give thee here no jot of blood; The words expressly are 'a pound of flesh:'
quotations.speaker: Portia
quotations.context: Stopping Shylock as he prepares to cut.
quotations.analysis: She has let the case run to the point of the knife before producing the objection, which means the trap was set several hundred lines earlier. Her method is a stricter literalism than Shylock’s own, with no mercy in it: he asked for what the words say, and she gives him exactly that and no more.

quotations.text: Nay, take my life and all; pardon not that: You take my house when you do take the prop That doth sustain my house; you take my life When you do take the means whereby I live.
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: After the court has divided his estate and offered to commute the fine.
quotations.analysis: With ‘take’ four times in four lines, the verdict reads like an inventory. He refuses the distinction the court is congratulating itself on — between killing a man and removing his livelihood — and the play gives him the argument without letting him win it.

quotations.text: Two things provided more, that, for this favour, He presently become a Christian;
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: Stating his terms for giving up his half of Shylock's goods.
quotations.analysis: It is called a favour, and it is attached as a condition to a pardon Shylock cannot refuse. 'Presently' means at once: the man who has just been prevented from taking a pound of flesh is required to change religion on the spot, and the scene treats this as the merciful outcome.

quotations.text: I am content.
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Asked by Portia whether he accepts the court's terms.
quotations.analysis: Three words, and then four more lines asking to be allowed to leave because he is not well. Antonio had used the same phrase twelve lines earlier while dictating the terms, so the play puts the identical sentence in two mouths in one scene and lets the difference between them stand without comment.

quotations.text: How sweet the moonlight sleeps upon this bank! Here will we sit and let the sounds of music Creep in our ears:
quotations.speaker: Lorenzo
quotations.context: In the garden at Belmont with Jessica, waiting for Portia's return.
quotations.analysis: The last act opens by changing the weather completely: after four hundred lines of courtroom prose the play produces its most lyrical verse, and does it in the mouth of the man who organised the elopement and the theft. Shakespeare buys the comedy its ending with music, and the person who says she is never merry when she hears it is sitting next to him.

quotations.text: I am never merry when I hear sweet music.
quotations.speaker: Jessica
quotations.context: Her reply to Lorenzo's account of music's power over wild animals.
quotations.analysis: It is the last thing she says in the play. Lorenzo talks her out of it immediately, explaining that attentiveness only looks like sadness, and she does not answer — a silence that productions can play as agreement, exhaustion or something colder.

timeline.label: Il Pecorone reaches print
timeline.detail: Ser Giovanni Fiorentino's fourteenth-century collection contains the bond, the trial and the lady disguised as a lawyer.

timeline.label: Roderigo Lopez is executed in London
timeline.detail: The queen's Portuguese physician, of Jewish descent, was convicted of conspiracy; the trial fed a wave of public feeling in the years just before the play.

timeline.label: Entered in the Stationers' Register
timeline.detail: Registered to James Roberts as the Merchant of Venice, two years before it was printed.

timeline.label: First Quarto
timeline.detail: The earliest printed text, and the basis of most modern editions.

timeline.label: First recorded performance, at court
timeline.detail: The first recorded performance, on 10 February, with a repeat before the court two days later.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed among the comedies, following the quarto text closely.

timeline.label: Charles Macklin plays Shylock at Drury Lane
timeline.detail: He abandoned the comic red wig of the Restoration stage and played the part seriously, which changed the play's reputation.

timeline.label: Edmund Kean's London debut as Shylock
timeline.detail: A performance that made the moneylender a figure of tragic force, no longer a stage villain.

timeline.label: Henry Irving's Shylock at the Lyceum
timeline.detail: Irving's dignified, sympathetic reading dominated the late Victorian stage and shaped expectations for decades.

timeline.label: Michael Radford's film
timeline.detail: A screen version set in a carefully reconstructed Venice, with Al Pacino as Shylock and an opening sequence about the ghetto.

places.name: Venice
places.note: The city of the bond, the street insults and the court of justice.

places.name: The Rialto
places.note: The commercial exchange where news of ships travels and where Antonio has abused Shylock in public.

places.name: Genoa
places.note: Where Tubal reports Jessica spending her father's ducats and trading her mother's ring.

places.name: Padua
places.note: Home of Doctor Bellario, whose legal opinion and borrowed credentials get Portia into the courtroom.

places.name: Tripoli
places.note: One of the ports named for Antonio's argosies, and the destination of the ship reported lost.

criticalViews.position: A romantic comedy with an obstacle
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the play’s business is three marriages and a rescue, Shylock is the blocking figure whom comedy must remove, and Act V is the proper ending, not an evasion.
criticalViews.counter: It requires the audience to accept a forced conversion as a happy outcome, and it cannot explain why Shakespeare gave the obstacle the best prose in the play.

criticalViews.position: A play whose antisemitism is its subject, not an accident
criticalViews.summary: Much modern criticism argues that the Christians are shown behaving exactly as Shylock describes them — spitting, mocking, confiscating — so that the comedy is built to expose the society it flatters.
criticalViews.counter: The play still ends in that society's garden, with its victim offstage, and the text nowhere condemns what the court does.

criticalViews.position: A study of contract and obligation
criticalViews.summary: Bonds, wills, caskets and rings are all binding documents, and the play shows what happens when a written promise meets the intention behind it. The trial is then less about race than about how far a society will honour its own paperwork.
criticalViews.counter: The verdict turns on a statute about aliens, which makes Shylock's standing under Venetian law inseparable from his religion.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare present Shylock?
essayQuestions.focus: Sympathy, hostility and the limits of both
plan: Note first that he appears in only five scenes and never speaks after 4.1.412.
Use 1.3 to show him giving an itemised account of the abuse, and Antonio confirming every word of it.
Read 3.1 carefully: the questions establish common humanity, and the same logic then licenses revenge.
Set the reported grief of 2.8 against the direct speech of 4.1.388 and ask which the audience is allowed to trust.
Close on his exit line and on the fact that Act V does not mention him.

essayQuestions.question: 'Mercy in this play is something the powerful do to the powerless.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Justice, law and the trial scene
plan: Begin with Shylock's question at 4.1.190 — on what compulsion? — and show that Portia's speech is a direct answer to it.
Trace the reversal: mercy preached, refused, then imposed as a set of conditions at 4.1.394-404.
Examine the alien statute and what it says about who counts as a citizen of Venice.
Weigh Antonio's terms, including the conversion, against his conduct in 1.3.
Decide whether the play endorses the verdict, exposes it, or simply stages it and moves on.

essayQuestions.question: What is the function of Belmont?
essayQuestions.focus: Place, wealth and the structure of the play
plan: Set out the alternation: Venice for business and law, Belmont for music, riddles and marriage.
Show that Belmont is also governed by a document — a dead man's will — and so is less free than it looks.
Use the casket scenes to argue that the two worlds share one question: how do you value what you cannot see?
Note that Portia's money resolves nothing in Venice; it is her legal reading that wins.
Judge whether Act V restores Belmont or merely relocates the play's unfinished business.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of women in The Merchant of Venice.
essayQuestions.focus: Portia, Nerissa, Jessica and the uses of disguise
plan: Start from the constraint: Portia cannot choose, Jessica is locked in, Nerissa marries where her mistress does.
Show disguise as the only available instrument — a boy's coat for one, a doctor's gown for another.
Read the trial as Portia acquiring, temporarily, a competence the play otherwise reserves for men.
Use the ring plot to argue that she brings the courtroom's methods home with her.
Ask what happens to that competence in Act V, when the gowns come off.

discussionQuestions: Antonio never explains his sadness. Should a production decide what it is?
Shylock's greatest speech ends by promising revenge. Does that ending change what the speech is worth?
Portia argues that mercy cannot be compelled, and then compels it. Is she a hypocrite, or is the court?
Jessica's last line is that she is never merry when she hears sweet music. What should she do for the rest of the scene?
The play is classed as a comedy. What would have to change for it to be a tragedy?

related.why: The other Venetian play, and the other outsider whom the city uses and then discards.
A comedy that also stops for a long argument about mercy and the letter of the law, and also ends in silence.
Another heroine who puts on a man's clothes, with the same interest in what a disguise makes possible.
The other great breeches role of these years, in a comedy that uses the same device and pushes it in the opposite direction.
A comedy of the same period that comes close to tragedy for a whole act before recovering.
